analysis.one_liner: Hands PolyMet Mining 6,650 acres of Superior National Forest for its copper-nickel mine project.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee markup or floor vote and died when the 116th Congress ended, despite the Forest Service having already approved the same land exchange in its January 2017 Record of Decision.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would order the federal government to swap 6,650 acres of Superior National Forest land in Minnesota to PolyMet Mining in exchange for 6,690 acres of PolyMet's land, completing the deal within 90 days of passage. The swap is the land PolyMet needs for its proposed NorthMet copper-nickel mine. The bill would lock in 2015 appraisals, bar any reappraisal, and replace the normal land-exchange process with a direct congressional mandate. It was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: PolyMet Mining Corporation, the company behind the proposed NorthMet copper-nickel mine. The bill would hand the company the federal land parcel its mine sits on, at essentially no cash cost — the appraisals found the government actually owed PolyMet $425,000 to even out the values, which PolyMet would waive [S2] [S3]. It would also shorten the process to 90 days, lock in the 2015 appraisals so they could never be redone, and eliminate the risk of court challenges to the exchange, which the bill's own findings describe as 'avoid[ing] potential litigation' [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: PolyMet Mining and its mine project

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs the Secretary of Agriculture to accept PolyMet's offer and convey the 6,650-acre federal parcel 'not later than 90 days after the date of enactment,' removing the normal discretionary review process [S3] [S2].
It fixes the 2015 appraised values as the values for the exchange and states they 'shall not be subject to reappraisal,' so the land's worth could never be reexamined [S3].

The bill's own findings say the exchange would 'provide a practical resolution to complex issues pertaining to the development of private mineral rights underlying the Federal land surface, and thereby avoid potential litigation' — removing a legal threat to the mine project [S3].

Supporters, including the region's Republican congressman and the district's Democratic congressman, framed the deal as good for the mining-region economy: the federal parcel sits next to existing iron-mining infrastructure, and the swap adds 6,500-plus acres to the public forest with new access [S3] [S4].

analysis.who_pays: The public. The federal parcel — land bought under the Weeks Act for the national forest — would become private land 'available for any lawful use' under mining laws [S3]. The land would be the site of a copper-nickel sulfide mine, a type of mining that carries well-known risks of acid mine drainage into nearby waters, including the Lake Superior watershed. The public would also forgo any chance of a reappraisal of the land's value before the deal closed.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, which loses federal forest land

drawbacks.text: The bill overrides the standard land-exchange process, which normally leaves appraisal and timing decisions to the agency; locking in 2015 appraisals and barring reappraisal means the public would never learn the land's current value before conveying it [S3].

The 90-day deadline and automatic revocation of land withdrawals leave no room for further federal review; the federal parcel becomes 'available for any lawful use in accordance with... laws and regulations that pertain to mining,' placing sulfide-mining activity on former national forest land [S3].

The honest counter-case, which the bill itself makes: the Forest Service had already issued a Final Record of Decision on January 9, 2017 approving this exact exchange after review, and the swap yields a 40-acre net gain of federal land, reduces ownership boundaries by 33 miles, and acquires 307 acres for ecological research areas [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public does get something back — 6,690 acres added to the forest, with a small net gain in acreage — and the exchange was not invented by Congress; it had already survived a federal environmental review and Record of Decision. But the bill is structured entirely for the company's convenience: a 90-day deadline, frozen appraisals, no reappraisal, and automatic legal cover against litigation. A land deal of this size would normally allow the values to be rechecked before closing; this bill forbids it. The downside — permanent public loss of the forest parcel and its transfer to private mining use — lasts forever, while the public's side of the trade is fixed at 2015 paper values.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in January 2019, referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and then to its National Parks subcommittee, and sat there until the 116th Congress ended in January 2021 without a markup or floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Pete Stauber introduced the bill on January 14, 2019, and it was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources the same day [S5] [S1].
On February 4, 2019, it was referred to the Subcommittee on National Parks, Forests, and Public Lands; no markup, hearing, or floor vote followed in the action history [S5].
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and the bill never advanced past subcommittee referral [S5].

The land exchange itself had already been approved at the administrative level: the bill's definitions cite a Final Record of Decision issued by the Forest Service on January 9, 2017 approving the NorthMet land exchange between the United States and PolyMet [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: PolyMet Mining was not left empty-handed by this bill's death: the Forest Service's 2017 Record of Decision approving the same exchange remained in place, so the company could pursue the deal through the administrative process the bill was trying to shortcut [S3]. Ordinary people came out ahead only in the narrow sense that the appraisal freeze and 90-day mandate never became law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: PolyMet Mining, via its existing administrative approval

for.name: Rep. Pete Stauber
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill directing the Forest Service to complete the PolyMet land exchange within 90 days of enactment.

for.name: Rep. Collin Peterson
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill and was named in its introduction as an original cosponsor.

against.name: Rep. Raúl Grijalva
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup of the bill; it sat at subcommittee referral for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Conservation groups opposing the PolyMet mine
against.what_they_did: Opposed the NorthMet project and the land transfer on water-quality and public-lands grounds, keeping the exchange politically contested.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and 8 of the bill's 9 cosponsors were Republicans, joined by one Democrat (Rep. Collin Peterson) whose district includes mining country; the bill then died without a vote in the House Natural Resources Committee, which Democrats chaired in this Congress.

industries.industry: Metals mining (PolyMet Mining Corp. and the copper-nickel sector)
industries.note: The bill would convey the federal parcel PolyMet needs for its NorthMet mine, lock in 2015 appraisals with no reappraisal, and give the company a 90-day congressional mandate shielding the deal from further review or litigation. The public pays with permanent loss of the forest parcel and the environmental risk of sulfide mining beside it.

Supporters from both parties presented the exchange as a job creator for the mining region, since the federal parcel sits beside existing mining infrastructure. That benefit flows to a specific region and industry rather than to the public at large, and it comes bundled with the land transfer to PolyMet.

The bill takes 6,650 acres of national forest out of public ownership — land that becomes a private mine site — but adds 6,690 acres of PolyMet land to the forest, which the bill's findings say comes with new public access on parcels that previously had none. Recreation users bear the permanent loss of the mine-site parcel.
